chapter_title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Server Management

screens.title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) Server Management
screens.subtitle: Automate IP addressing, manage reservations, relay across subnets, and secure DHCP services

narration.text: In this chapter you will master DHCP server management using the ISC DHCP implementation common on Linux systems. We'll explain how the dhcpd. conf file determines leases, ranges, gateways and DNS, and how to create static reservations so a printer or server always gets the same address. You'll also learn how PXE boot uses filename and next-server options to deliver network boot information, and how relay agents extend DHCP across subnets without placing a server in each VLAN. Practical troubleshooting steps are included: where to read leases, which ports must be open, and how to interpret server logs when leases fail or addresses conflict. Finally, we'll cover basic security controls that reduce the risk of rogue DHCP servers and MAC spoofing, such as firewall rules, file permissions, and switch-level DHCP snooping. By the end you will be able to configure a working dhcpd. conf, enable services on the right interface, add reservations for critical devices, set up a relay agent, and perform first-line troubleshooting and mitigation. As you follow along, think about a device in your environment that needs a fixed address and how you would reserve it with a host block.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: DHCP centralizes network configuration: dhcpd.conf defines who gets which IP, options control gateway/DNS/PXE behavior, and relay agents allow a single server to serve multiple subnets while logs and leases aid troubleshooting.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll demonstrate by the end of this chapter — part 1

narration.text: First, we'll focus on practical configuration and core operational skills. You will learn to author and manage the ISC dhcpd. conf file so clients receive IP addresses, subnet masks, gateways and DNS servers automatically. This includes writing subnet declarations, defining a lease range, and setting global options such as domain-name-servers. You'll also learn to implement static reservations using the host block and a client's MAC address so critical devices keep predictable addresses. A third objective is preparing PXE boot options: you'll specify the boot filename and next-server IP to enable network-based OS provisioning. Finally, you'll practice making the DHCP service listen on the correct interface and start and enable the systemd service so the server begins serving leases after boot. Each objective includes a concrete verification step so you can confirm competency — for example, verifying a client receives an expected lease or that systemctl reports the service as active.

keyIdea.title: Practical setup
keyIdea.text: Authoring dhcpd.conf and managing the service are foundational tasks: they let dynamic addressing, reservations and PXE boot work reliably in production.

narration.text: Next, you will extend DHCP services across subnets using relay agents and learn how to configure dhcrelay or isc-dhcp-relay so clients on remote VLANs receive leases from a central server. Troubleshooting is another objective: you'll read dhcpd. leases, examine server logs, and check client dhclient output to diagnose lease issues, conflicts, or misconfigured ranges. You'll also learn defensive measures: open UDP ports 67 and 68 in the server firewall, restrict dhcpd files with proper filesystem permissions, and use switch-level DHCP snooping and port security to reduce the chance of rogue servers or MAC spoofing. Each objective ends with a verification activity, like confirming relay-forwarded leases appear on the server's lease file.

screens.title: DHCP fundamentals and the lease lifecycle (DORA)
screens.subtitle: How clients request addresses and what a lease represents

narration.text: DHCP is the protocol that automates IP addressing and related configuration. At its heart is the lease lifecycle: Discover, Offer, Request, and Acknowledge — often referred to as DORA. A client broadcasts a Discover to find servers. Any DHCP server that can serve the client's subnet replies with an Offer that includes a candidate IP address and options like gateway and DNS. The client then sends a Request indicating which Offer it accepts. Finally the server responds with an Acknowledge and records the lease in dhcpd. leases. A lease is time-limited; the client must renew it periodically. A concrete example: a laptop connects to a wired port and sends a broadcast Discover. The server offers 192.168.30.157 with option routers 192.168.30.1 and domain-name-servers 192.168.30.100. The laptop requests that address and the server acknowledges, adding an entry to /var/lib/dhcpd/dhcpd. leases with timestamps and the client's MAC. A common misconception is that DHCP assigns permanent addresses; leases are temporary unless you configure a host reservation. Another pitfall is assuming broadcasts cross routers — they do not, which is why relay agents exist. Key practice: watch journalctl -u dhcpd during DORA to see Offers and Acks, and inspect dhcpd. leases to confirm active leases and timestamps. What device in your environment should have a reservation rather than a dynamic lease?

keyIdea.title: DORA & leases
keyIdea.text: Discover-Offer-Request-Acknowledge defines how DHCP assigns time-bound addresses; leases are recorded in dhcpd.leases and must be renewed.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › DHCP fundamentals
DORA: Discover → Offer → Request → Acknowledge
Clients and servers exchange four messages to negotiate a time-limited lease. The server records leases for tracking and conflict avoidance.
Concrete example
A laptop broadcasts Discover. Server offers 192.168.30.157. Laptop requests it. Server acknowledges and writes to dhcpd.leases.
Common misconception
Leases are temporary by default; reservations are required for permanent addresses.
Quick checks
  • Use journalctl -u dhcpd to watch Offers and Acks in real time.
  • Open /var/lib/dhcpd/dhcpd.leases to inspect lease timestamps and MAC bindings.
  • Confirm renewals by observing client dhclient output when renewing a lease.
Annotated flow
Discover
Client broadcast to find servers; contains client MAC.
Offer
Server replies with candidate IP and options like routers and DNS.
Request
Client asks to accept the server's offered address.
Acknowledge
Server confirms, updates dhcpd.leases, and the client configures its interface.
Key Takeaway

DORA is the handshake that creates time-bound leases; inspect dhcpd.leases and server logs to validate behavior.

screens.title: Examining dhcpd.conf: global settings and subnet declarations
screens.subtitle: Authoring options, ranges, and lease times for a working server

narration.text: The dhcpd. conf file drives ISC DHCP server behavior. At the top you'll often see global directives like ddns-update-style, ignore client-updates, and default-lease-time plus max-lease-time to control default lease durations. Global option stanzas set domain-name, domain-name-servers and optional services such as NTP servers. Subnet declarations then define which addresses the server can hand out for a given network. A typical subnet block declares the network and netmask, a range for dynamic leases, the routers option for the default gateway, and broadcast-address. For PXE boot you add filename and next-server inside the subnet. A concrete configuration example is shown in the code panel on this screen: it uses a 192.168.20.0/24 net with range 192.168.20.100–199 and a host reservation at.200. A common mistake is placing a static fixed-address inside the dynamic range — this can create conflicts. After editing dhcpd. conf, run a syntax or dry-run check if your distribution offers one, then restart the dhcpd service to apply changes. When you test, verify clients receive the intended gateway and DNS. How would you restructure the file if you needed per-subnet NTP servers?

keyIdea.title: dhcpd.conf structure
keyIdea.text: Global directives set defaults; subnet blocks specify ranges and options. Keep reservations outside dynamic ranges to avoid conflicts.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › dhcpd.conf Walkthrough
Example dhcpd.conf
This snippet demonstrates global options, a subnet block, and a host reservation used in many labs and production setups.
# /etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf
ddns-update-style interim;
ignore client-updates;
default-lease-time 600;
max-lease-time 7200;

option domain-name "example.com";
option domain-name-servers 192.168.20.10, 8.8.8.8;
option ntp-servers 192.168.20.10;

subnet 192.168.20.0 netmask 255.255.255.0 {
    range 192.168.20.100 192.168.20.199;
    option routers 192.168.20.1;
    option broadcast-address 192.168.20.255;
    # filename "pxelinux.0";
    # next-server 192.168.20.50;
}

host webserver {
    hardware ethernet 00:11:22:33:44:55;
    fixed-address 192.168.20.200;
}
Explainer
  • default-lease-time and max-lease-time control how long clients keep an address by default.
  • option domain-name-servers lists resolvers clients receive; include local and public DNS as needed.
  • Keep host reservations (fixed-address) outside the dynamic range to avoid accidental conflicts.
Example scenario
If a PXE server at 192.168.20.50 provides installers, uncomment filename and next-server so clients learn the boot file and TFTP server IP during the Offer step.
Key Takeaway

dhcpd.conf is layered: globals set defaults and subnet blocks define concrete address assignments and options for each network.

screens.title: Bind the server to an interface and manage the dhcpd service
screens.subtitle: Specify listening interfaces and use systemd to enable the DHCP server

narration.text: After authoring dhcpd. conf, the ISC DHCP server must be told which interfaces to serve. Debian/Ubuntu uses /etc/default/isc-dhcp-server with INTERFACESv4 set to the interface name, for example INTERFACESv4="eth0". RHEL/CentOS uses /etc/sysconfig/dhcpd and the DHCPDARGS variable in a similar way. Once interfaces are set, enable and start the service with systemctl enable --now dhcpd (or isc-dhcp-server on Debian). Confirm the unit is active and check journalctl -u dhcpd for errors during startup. If clients still do not receive leases, ensure UDP ports 67 and 68 are allowed by your firewall — for firewalld use firewall-cmd --add-service=dhcp --permanent and reload. A practical sequence: set interface, run systemctl restart, check systemctl status, tail journalctl -u dhcpd, and verify a client obtains an address. A common error is forgetting to configure INTERFACES and seeing a server that is active but not listening on the expected network. Another issue is SELinux or apparmor denial; those can be diagnosed in audit logs. The final step is to test with a client and use dhclient -v on the client to observe DORA messages and confirm option delivery. What command would you run first to confirm the service is enabled at boot?

keyIdea.title: Service lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Set the interface variable, enable the systemd unit, and verify logs and firewall rules so the server accepts client broadcasts and serves leases.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Service & Interfaces
Configure interface
Debian/Ubuntu: edit /etc/default/isc-dhcp-server and set INTERFACESv4="eth0". RHEL/CentOS: edit /etc/sysconfig/dhcpd and set DHCPDARGS="eth0".
Operational checklist
  • Save config and restart the service: sudo systemctl restart dhcpd
  • Enable at boot: sudo systemctl enable --now dhcpd
  • Inspect logs: sudo journalctl -u dhcpd -f
  • Verify client: on client run sudo dhclient -v or check network manager logs
Firewall & ports
DHCP uses UDP 67 for server and UDP 68 for clients. With firewalld, run:
sudo firewall-cmd --add-service=dhcp --permanent
sudo firewall-cmd --reload
Common mistake

The service may appear active but not serve clients if INTERFACES is blank or firewall blocks UDP 67/68; always check both.

Key Takeaway

Binding to the correct interface and allowing UDP 67/68 are essential operational steps before client verification.

screens.title: Static reservations (host blocks) and when to use them
screens.subtitle: Guarantee persistent addresses for servers, printers and infrastructure

narration.text: Static reservations, implemented as host blocks, let the DHCP server always hand the same IP to a device based on its MAC address. Reservations are ideal for devices that require stable addressing such as printers, management interfaces, network storage, or PXE servers. The host block lists the hardware ethernet MAC and a fixed-address. For example, mapping 00:11:22:33:44:55 to 192.168.20.200 ensures that device always receives that IP via DHCP. A key advantage is centralized management: network teams maintain addresses in dhcpd. conf rather than configuring static addresses on every device. A common error is placing the fixed-address within the dynamic range — which can allow the server to also hand that address to another client. Best practice: choose a reserved pool outside the dynamic range or adjust ranges accordingly. Also consider file permissions and who can edit dhcpd. conf to prevent unauthorized reservations. When testing, change a virtual client's MAC to the reserved MAC and renew the lease to confirm receipt of the fixed-address. Misunderstanding that static reservations bypass DHCP entirely is false — they still use the DHCP flow but the server recognizes the MAC and assigns the preconfigured IP. Reflect: which devices in your environment would benefit most from reservations?

keyIdea.title: Reservations
keyIdea.text: Host blocks bind MAC addresses to fixed-address values; keep reservations outside dynamic ranges and verify with a client lease renewal.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Static Reservations
Host reservation example
host myprinter {
    hardware ethernet AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF;    # REPLACE with actual MAC
    fixed-address 192.168.30.201;
}
Save and restart dhcpd so the reservation takes effect, then trigger a client renewal to get the fixed address.
When to reserve
  • Servers and management interfaces
  • Network printers and NAS devices
  • PXE/TFTP servers that clients must reach reliably
Avoid this mistake
Do not place fixed-address entries inside the dynamic range. Instead move the reservation outside the range or shrink the range.
Key Takeaway

Reservations centralize stable addressing via DHCP; they still participate in the lease flow but always receive the configured fixed-address.

screens.title: PXE boot with filename and next-server
screens.subtitle: How DHCP provides boot file and TFTP server IP for network installs

narration.text: PXE boot relies on DHCP to supply two pieces of information: the boot filename and the TFTP server IP. The filename option names the bootloader image such as pxelinux.0, and next-server points clients to the TFTP server's IP address. When a PXE-enabled client boots, it runs DORA and picks up the Offer that includes filename and next-server; it then contacts the TFTP server to fetch the boot program. This is commonly used to provision diskless machines or to automate OS installation at scale. A practical example from the configuration earlier includes filename "pxelinux.0" and next-server 192.168.20.50 in the subnet block. Be aware that inconsistent next-server values or incorrect TFTP configuration are common causes of PXE failures. Also confirm firewall and router ACLs permit TFTP and DHCP traffic between client and server when they are in different subnets. One misconception is thinking TFTP is delivered by DHCP — DHCP only tells the client where to find it. The takeaway is to coordinate DHCP options with a properly configured TFTP service and verify by observing the client's boot logs or TFTP access logs. If the client never fetches the file, check both DHCP Offers for filename and next-server and the TFTP server's accessibility.

keyIdea.title: PXE options
keyIdea.text: filename and next-server let DHCP point PXE clients to a boot file and TFTP server; DHCP supplies pointers, TFTP serves the file.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › PXE Options
What DHCP tells PXE clients
DHCP provides pointers: filename indicates the boot file; next-server is the TFTP server IP. Both must be reachable for PXE to succeed.
Example
In the subnet block include: filename "pxelinux.0"; next-server 192.168.20.50; so clients learn the TFTP server and boot file during DHCP Offer.
Misconception
DHCP only points to TFTP. The TFTP server must be configured and accessible for the client to fetch the boot file.
Checklist for PXE
  • Set filename and next-server in dhcpd.conf
  • Ensure TFTP server is reachable and serves the file
  • Open TFTP and DHCP ports in firewall
Troubleshoot
If PXE fails, inspect DHCP Offers for filename/next-server and test TFTP access from a host on the same network segment.
Key Takeaway

DHCP supplies pointers for PXE; coordinate DHCP options with a functioning TFTP server to enable network booting.

screens.title: DHCP relay agents: extend DHCP across subnets
screens.subtitle: How relays forward broadcasts to a central DHCP server

narration.text: DHCP is broadcast-based and clients broadcast Discover messages that do not cross routers. To serve multiple subnets with one DHCP server you use a relay agent. A relay agent listens for broadcasts on the client subnet, wraps them as unicast messages, and forwards them to the server's IP. Common implementations are dhcrelay or isc-dhcp-relay. On the relay machine configure the client-facing interface and list the DHCP server IP to forward to; for example dhcrelay -i eth0 192.168.30.100 or editing /etc/default/isc-dhcp-relay with INTERFACESv4 and SERVERS. When the server replies, the relay agent forwards the response back to the originating subnet. A concrete scenario: Server A on 192.168.30.0/24 serves addresses; Relay B on 192.168.40.0/24 runs dhcrelay listening on eth0 and forwards client requests to 192.168.30.100. Client on 192.168.40.0/24 receives a lease from Server A. Typical mistakes include forwarding from the wrong interface or forgetting to open UDP 67/68 on the relay host's firewall. Use journalctl on both relay and server to confirm Discover messages arrive at the server and Offers return via the relay. Finally, ensure router or firewall ACLs permit the unicast traffic between relay and server. How could you confirm a Discover from a client reached the server?

keyIdea.title: Relay function
keyIdea.text: Relay agents convert client broadcasts into unicast messages to a DHCP server, enabling one server to serve multiple subnets.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › DHCP Relay Agents
Relay configuration examples
RHEL/CentOS: set /etc/sysconfig/dhcrelay DHCP server IP(s) and interface. Debian/Ubuntu: edit /etc/default/isc-dhcp-relay with INTERFACESv4 and SERVERS.
# Example runtime command
sudo dhcrelay -i eth0 192.168.30.100

# Debian config snippet
INTERFACESv4="eth0"
SERVERS="192.168.30.100"
Verification steps
  • Tail journalctl on the relay: discover messages should be logged.
  • Check server logs for the forwarded request and subsequent Offer.
  • Confirm client received a lease from the server's range.
Watch out
If you see no Offers at the server, verify relay is listening on the correct interface and that network ACLs allow traffic to the server.
Key Takeaway

Relays forward client broadcasts as unicast to servers; confirm interface, server IP, and firewall rules to ensure proper forwarding.

screens.title: Common DHCP failures and logfile forensics
screens.subtitle: Use dhcpd.leases, journalctl, and client tools to locate root causes

narration.text: Troubleshooting DHCP requires checking both server-side artifacts and client behavior. On the server, dhcpd. leases stores lease history and active bindings: inspect it to see which MAC holds which IP and lease timestamps. Use journalctl -u dhcpd to find configuration errors, binding failures, or duplicate server announcements. On clients, run dhclient -v or check ip a to examine assigned addresses and lease renewal attempts. Typical misconfigurations are overlapping ranges that lead to duplicate assignments, incorrect netmask values that place hosts in the wrong subnet, or multiple DHCP servers on the same segment sending competing Offers. IP conflicts often arise when a manual static IP is placed inside the DHCP range — check dhcpd. leases and the client network settings in that case. If relays are used, verify that the server receives the forwarded Discover by looking for the relay agent's identifier in the server logs. Firewall blocks on UDP 67/68 are another frequent cause; test connectivity by temporarily allowing the dhcp service through the server and relay firewalls. Finally, if leases appear stale, consider whether the lease file path is correct for your distribution; many servers keep leases under /var/lib/dhcpd or /var/lib/dhcp. When you diagnose an issue, isolate by testing a single client with verbose logging and follow the log entries from Discover to Acknowledge.

keyIdea.title: Forensics & fixes
keyIdea.text: Combine dhcpd.leases, journalctl, and client dhclient output to pinpoint misconfigurations like overlapping ranges, blocked ports, or rogue servers.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Troubleshooting
Server-side artifacts
  • dhcpd.leases: current and historical lease entries; check MAC, IP, and timestamps.
  • journalctl -u dhcpd: runtime errors, binding problems, and option parsing messages.
  • /var/log/messages or syslog: additional DHCP server messages on some distros.
Client-side checks
On the client, use dhclient -v to observe Discover/Offer/Request/Ack. Use ip a to confirm the assigned address and route table. For conflicts, look for duplicate-address warnings and verify that no static IP lives inside the DHCP range.
Quick diagnostic

If a client gets no IP, check relay logs, server logs, firewall rules and confirm the server is bound to the correct interface.

screens.title: Preventing rogue servers and MAC spoofing
screens.subtitle: Practical measures: firewall rules, file protection, and switch-level controls

narration.text: Securing DHCP focuses on preventing unauthorized servers and limiting MAC spoofing. Rogue DHCP servers can hand out malicious gateways or DNS and disrupt networks. Start with basic host hardening: restrict read/write access to dhcpd. conf and dhcpd. leases to administrative users. Ensure your firewall only allows UDP 67/68 from trusted interfaces or relay hosts. On switches, enable DHCP snooping where supported; it tracks trusted ports and discards DHCP server messages from untrusted ports, blocking rogue offers. Port security on access ports can limit which MAC addresses are allowed and reduce spoofing of reserved MACs. These switch-level features are not a replacement for careful server configuration but they significantly raise the bar against an attacker. For reserved devices, combine host reservations with switch port bindings so only the device with the expected MAC can use that port. A common misconception is that file permissions alone are sufficient — they protect the server but do not stop a rogue server on the same VLAN. Use layered controls: service firewalling, file access, and switch policies. After applying protections, test by attempting to introduce a second DHCP server in a lab and confirming the network ignores its Offers when DHCP snooping is enabled.

keyIdea.title: Layered protections
keyIdea.text: Combine file permissions, firewall rules, and switch DHCP snooping/port security to reduce rogue DHCP servers and MAC spoofing risks.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › DHCP Security
Server hardening
  • Protect /etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf and the lease file with restrictive permissions.
  • Limit which hosts can reach the DHCP service via firewall rules.
  • Audit changes to dhcpd.conf and the lease file regularly.
Switch-level controls
  • Enable DHCP snooping to mark trusted ports and filter server Offers from untrusted ports.
  • Use port security to lock ports to expected MAC addresses for critical devices.
  • Combine switch features with server-side controls for layered defense.
Misconception

File permissions alone do not stop rogue servers on the network; use switch-level features to reject unauthorized DHCP Offers.

screens.title: Terminal-first lab walkthrough: configure server, reservation and relay
screens.subtitle: Step through edits, start services, and verify client leases using terminal examples

narration.text: This lab follows a terminal-first flow. Begin by installing the ISC DHCP server package for your distribution. Edit /etc/dhcp/dhcpd. conf to define global options, a subnet with range, and a host reservation. For example, set default-lease-time and domain-name-servers and add a subnet 192.168.30.0/24 with range 192.168.30.150–199 and a host block for a printer MAC. Next set the listening interface: on Debian update /etc/default/isc-dhcp-server INTERFACESv4="eth0", on RHEL set DHCPDARGS. Start the service with sudo systemctl enable --now dhcpd and watch journalctl -u dhcpd -f while a test client requests a lease. For the relay agent, install isc-dhcp-relay or dhcrelay on the relay host, configure it to listen on the client-facing interface and forward to the server IP, then enable and start the relay service. Verify the client on the remote subnet receives an IP from the server's range and that the server's dhcpd. leases contains the client's MAC and assigned IP. A specific test: change the test client's MAC to the reserved MAC and renew the lease; the client should now receive the fixed-address. This sequence ensures configuration, service binding, relay forwarding, and reservation behavior all work end-to-end.

keyIdea.title: Lab flow
keyIdea.text: Install, edit dhcpd.conf, set interface variables, start server, configure relay, then verify leases and reservations from client renewals.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Lab Walkthrough
Server steps (example commands)
Follow these terminal actions as a checklist. Replace interface and IP values with your environment specifics.
# Install (RHEL/CentOS)
sudo dnf install dhcp-server
# or Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt install isc-dhcp-server

# Edit /etc/dhcp/dhcpd.conf and add subnet + reservation

# Set interface
# Debian: /etc/default/isc-dhcp-server
INTERFACESv4="eth0"

# Start and enable
sudo systemctl enable --now dhcpd
# Watch logs
sudo journalctl -u dhcpd -f
Relay steps
Install dhcrelay or isc-dhcp-relay and configure to listen on the client-facing interface and forward to the DHCP server IP.
# Runtime example
sudo dhcrelay -i eth0 192.168.30.100

# Debian config: /etc/default/isc-dhcp-relay
INTERFACESv4="eth0"
SERVERS="192.168.30.100"
Verification
  • On client: sudo dhclient -v to request a lease and watch DORA
  • Confirm dhcpd.leases on server has the client MAC and IP
  • Change client MAC to reserved MAC and renew — confirm fixed-address assignment

screens.title: Verification checklist and common best practices
screens.subtitle: A tactical checklist to validate DHCP deployments and avoid pitfalls

narration.text: Before you declare a DHCP deployment complete, run a short verification checklist. First, confirm dhcpd. conf parses and that server starts cleanly. Next verify the server is bound to intended interfaces and firewall rules allow UDP 67/68. Then test a client: ensure it receives an IP from the configured range, correct gateway and DNS settings. Check dhcpd. leases to ensure the client's MAC and IP are recorded. For reservations, change a test client's MAC to the reserved MAC and renew the lease to ensure the fixed-address is granted. For relay agents, confirm that Discover messages are visible on the server logs and that Offers are relayed back to the client subnet. Monitor for common mistakes: overlapping ranges with other DHCP servers, incorrect netmasks, and lease times set too short for your environment. Best practices include keeping reservations outside dynamic pools, documenting reserved IPs, enabling DHCP snooping on switches where possible, and maintaining restricted edit access to dhcpd. conf and lease files. A short post-deployment monitoring window of logs and client checks helps catch intermittent issues before they affect users. Which step will you add to your standard checklist?

narration.text: These three core concepts summarize what matters for DHCP server management. First, dhcpd. conf is the authoritative source: global options, subnet blocks, ranges, and host reservations determine how addresses and options are assigned. Second, relay agents convert client broadcasts into unicasts to a central server, enabling one server to serve many subnets; relays must be configured to listen on the client interface and forward to the server IP. Third, diagnosis and security: dhcpd. leases and server logs are your primary forensic artifacts, and layered protections such as firewall rules, file permissions, and switch DHCP snooping reduce the risk of rogue servers and MAC spoofing. Keep these ideas in mind when you design, deploy, and troubleshoot DHCP services. Summary

screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders before you configure

narration.text: Keep these three reminders handy as you work: always place host reservations outside dynamic ranges to avoid conflicts; open UDP ports 67 and 68 on servers and relays so DHCP traffic can flow; and use switch-level DHCP snooping and port security in combination with server-side controls to limit rogue servers and MAC spoofing. Each of these small practices eliminates a common, high-impact failure mode and improves operational stability when DHCP serves many clients across multiple subnets.
